description:
We’re a 3-person family team from Honolulu, Hawaiʻi. We love music, science, and technology. Our team includes a high school 10th grader who loves computer science and sings opera, a mom who is a science nerd with a talent for music, and a dad who works at an education nonprofit.

Our team is named after a local bird, the Kōlea, which makes an amazing migration across the Pacific between Alaska and Hawaiʻi every year. We're Kōlea Sound Lab!
summary: We built an interactive website (Kīlauea in Concert) where visitors can experience NASA data visualizations more deeply, bringing them to life through music layers we composed. We were inspired by GEOS aerosols imagery of a 2024 Kīlauea volcano eruption, which sent sulfate particles into the air. We wrote code to analyze image colors, identify patterns, and trigger multiple musical layers. We wanted to bring the scientific data to life through music so a general audience could feel atmospheric change as well as see it. We also emphasized accessibility, using sound to make atmospheric patterns more accessible to people with visual impairments.
details:
Kīlauea in Concert turns patterns in NASA’s GEOS aerosol imagery into music through an interactive website.

How it works: Our code identifies and tracks green sulfate and cyan sea salt patterns in NASA’s GEOS visualization imagery from August–September 2024. Their positions and patterns trigger strings, harp, and choir voices. Visitors can play, pause, and reveal the visual guides behind the music. Note: We analyze rendered image colors, rather than direct sulfate measurements, to line up sound with specific visuals.

Benefits and intended impact: We want a general audience to feel atmospheric change as well as see it. Music provides another way to notice patterns and connect humans with the Earth. We hope that it increases understanding of how our world works and would love our approach to be extended to all EIC imagery. Our GitHub project shares a small, hands-on example of how we turn colors in NASA imagery into musical notes.

Data processing of images: We sampled still frames from NASA’s video, measured their visible green and cyan pixels, and saved those patterns as data that guides the music.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, and Web Audio. We used free and licensed instrument samples and OpenAI Codex assistance for coding, documentation, and testing.

Creativity: The music responds to changing visual patterns. Visitors can reveal tracked plumes and a musical grid to explore how movement becomes sound. We translate changing visual patterns into four musical layers: strings, harp, choir, and wind sounds, with up to three independently tracked plume voices. All ideas for how to translate imagery into sound were created by members of our team!

Accessibility: Throughout the project, we worked to make the experience understandable without sight: the music conveys movement in NASA’s imagery, while an optional spoken introduction, a plain-language listening guide, text descriptions of musical activity, keyboard controls, and a reduced-motion option offer other ways to explore it.

Design considerations: We considered all of these things: scientific accuracy, musical expression, source attribution, visual impaired accessibility. We attempted to include keyboard controls, screen-reader descriptions, and text labels alongside colors.
dataRefs: Science On A Sphere: Aerosols in the Air
